title: Chapter 72: The Unruly 1
content:
Chapter 72

The Unruly 1

Draped in flowing black robes, a pitch-black flute hung at his hip, its crimson tassel dangling like a drop of fresh blood. The newcomer tipped his head back and downed the wine in one clean swallow, turning the empty cup upside down to show Jin Zixun the dry porcelain bottom.

"I took it for him," he drawled, his voice lilting with a lazy smirk. "Satisfied?"

A roguish curve touched his lips, standing tall, effortlessly dashing, and commanding the room.

Lan Xichen called out, surprised, "Young Master Wei?"

A hushed murmur tore through the room: "When the hell did he get in here?!"

Wei Wuxian set the cup down, using one hand to casually straighten his collar. "Just now."

Just now? There had been no announcement at the gates, no footstep heard crossing the threshold. He had drifted into the heart of the Glamour Hall like a phantom, completely undetected. A collective shudder crept up the spines of the guests.

Jin Guangyao recovered in a heartbeat, plastering on his warmest, most welcoming facade. "We had no idea Young Master Wei was gracing Koi Tower with his presence, forgive our lack of hospitality! Shall we set a table for you? Ah, but where is your invitation?"

Wei Wuxian skipped the pleasantries, cutting straight to the bone. "Don't bother. Don't have one." He gave Jin Zixun a curt nod. "Young Master Jin. A word in private."

Jin Zixun sneered, "Whatever you've got to say, hold it until our banquet wraps up."

It was a blatant brush-off, and Wei Wuxian saw right through it. "How long am I supposed to wait?"

"Six or eight hours, maybe," Jin Zixun replied flippantly. "Ten, perhaps. Or try tomorrow."

"I don't have that kind of time."

Jin Zixun lifted his chin. "You'll wait whether you like it or not."

Jin Guangyao interjected gently, "May I ask what urgent business brings Young Master Wei to Zixun? Is it truly that pressing?"

Wei Wuxian’s eyes hardened. "Down to the wire. Every breath counts."

Ignoring him, Jin Zixun turned back to Lan Xichen, raising the second cup. "Sect Leader Lan, come on, you haven't finished yours yet!"

Seeing him deliberately dragging his feet, a dark, dangerous edge flickered across Wei Wuxian’s eyes. His lips curled into a razor-thin grin. "Fine. Then I'll air it right here. Tell me, Young Master Jin—do you know a man named Wen Ning?"

Jin Zixun scoffed, "Wen Ning? Never heard of him."

"You remember him," Wei Wuxian said, his tone dead even. "Last month, you were night-hunting around Ganquan, chasing an Eight-Winged Bat King straight into the settlement where the Wen remnants were rounded up. You dragged off a pack of Wen disciples, and the boy leading them was Wen Ning."

With the fall of the Qishan Wen Sect, their vast territories had been carved up like a roast among the victors, with Ganquan falling under the Lanling Jin banner. What was left of the Wen Clan had been herded into a desolate strip of Qishan, trapped on less than a fraction of a percent of their ancestral land, scraping by like cornered vermin.

Jin Zixun spat, "If I don't remember, I don't remember! I've got better things to do with my time than memorize the names of Wen dogs."

"Fine," Wei Wuxian replied smoothly. "Allow me to refresh your memory. You couldn't pin down that Bat King, and when a few Wen disciples wandered over to check out the disturbance, you forced Spirit-Attraction Flags onto their backs to use them as live bait. When they refused, one boy stepped forward, stammering his heart out to reason with you. That boy was Wen Ning. While you were busy arguing, the beast slipped away. You beat those disciples within an inch of their lives and dragged them off in chains. They haven't been seen since. Need any more details? They haven't returned home, and aside from you, I haven't the faintest clue who else to ask."

Jin Zixun sneered, "What's your game, Wei Wuxian? Demanding people from me? Don't tell me you're sticking your neck out for Wen dogs now?"

Wei Wuxian offered an easy, charming smile. "Does it matter if I'm sticking my neck out, or coming for yours? Hand them over."

With that last sentence, the warmth vanished from his face, his voice dropping into arctic silence. His patience was officially burnt to ash.

A heavy, instinctive chill washed over the room; even Jin Zixun’s scalp prickled with dread. But humiliation quickly stoked his temper, and he barked, "You've got some nerve, Wei Wuxian! Did the Lanling Jin Clan invite you today?! You dare strut into our hall and run your mouth? You honestly think you're invincible just because no one's dared cross you yet? You think you can overturn the heavens?!"

Wei Wuxian chuckled softly. "Equating yourself to the heavens? Forgive my bluntness, but your skin is a little thick for that."

Though Jin Zixun secretly regarded the Lanling Jin Clan as the new sky governing the world, he knew he’d let his arrogance slip too far. Fluster crept onto his cheeks, but before he could fire back, Jin Guangshan finally spoke from the high seat.

"Come now," Jin Guangshan chuckled easily. "It's hardly a matter worth losing our tempers over. Why work yourselves into such a state? Though, Young Master Wei, speaking fairly—crashing a private banquet hosted by my house is wildly out of line."

It was an open secret that Jin Guangshan was still fuming over the humiliation at the Phoenix Mountain hunt. That was why he’d sat back with an amused smirk while Jin Zixun picked a fight, only stepping in the moment his nephew started choking on his own words.

Wei Wuxian gave a curt nod. "Sect Leader Jin, I had no intention of crashing your gathering; pardon the intrusion. However, the men taken by Young Master Jin are missing, and a moment's delay could mean the difference between life and death. One of them saved my life, and I will not stand idly by. I ask for no leniency today; I will make amends another time."

"What cannot be pushed until tomorrow?" Jin Guangshan reasoned smoothly. "Come, take a seat, and we can discuss this properly."

Jin Guangyao had already orchestrated a fresh table setting behind them without making a sound.

Wei Wuxian declined flatly, "Thank you, Sect Leader Jin, but I'll pass. This cannot wait. Let us resolve it now."

"Haste makes waste," Jin Guangshan countered, his tone hardening under the pleasant veneer. "Strictly speaking, our clans have accounts of our own that have sat unsettled for far too long. Since you're here, why don't we clear the slate together?"

Wei Wuxian arched a brow. "Clear what slate?"

"Young Master Wei, we have touched on this matter a few times before. Surely you haven't forgotten... the weapon you wielded during the Sunshot Campaign?"

"Ah. You mean the Yin Tiger Tally. What about it?"

"Word has it that the Tally was forged from the refined spiritual iron of an ancient sword pulled from the belly of the Xuanwu of Slaughter," Jin Guangshan said evenly. "You unleashed it on the battlefield once, and its devastating malice caused catastrophic collateral damage to our own allies..."

Wei Wuxian cut him off. "Get to the point."

"That is the point. In that decisive battle, our forces suffered heavy casualties alongside the Wen Clan. An artifact of that nature defies conventional mastery. Entrusting it to the hands of a single individual... I fear that is hardly prudent."

Before the sentence even landed, Wei Wuxian burst into a sudden, clear laugh.

After a few mocking chuckles, he tilted his head. "Sect Leader Jin, humor me. Do you honestly believe that with the Qishan Wen Sect wiped off the board, the Lanling Jin Clan should naturally slide into their throne?"

A pin-drop silence choked the hall.

Wei Wuxian pressed, his voice razor-sharp, "Everything belongs to you? Everyone must bend to your whim? Watching the way your clan conducts itself, I almost mistook this for the golden age of the Wen tyrants."

A dark flush of humiliated fury swept across Jin Guangshan’s square jaw. Following the war, murmurs condemning Wei Wuxian’s demonic cultivation had begun quietly bubbling to the surface. He had brought up the Tally purely to dangle a collar over Wei Wuxian’s head—a subtle reminder that he had blood on his hands, that eyes were watching, that he shouldn't dream of trampling on the Jin Clan. He hadn't expected Wei Wuxian to strip the pretense away so brutally, leaving the raw, ugly ambition laid bare for the entire room to see.

A guest elder seated to Jin Guangshan’s right barked, "Wei Wuxian! Mind your tongue!"

"Did I lie?" Wei Wuxian shot back. "Using living captives as bait, crushing anyone who dares offer a whisper of defiance—how exactly is that different from what Qishan Wen pulled?!"

Another guest elder rose, sneering, "Of course it’s different! The Wen dogs committed monstrous atrocities; ending up like this is nothing less than divine retribution! We are merely returning an eye for an eye, letting them reap the bitter harvest they sowed themselves! What right do you have to scold us?!"

"An eye for an eye means taking it from the one who bit you," Wei Wuxian countered. "Wen Ning’s branch never had a speck of blood on their hands. Or are you telling me you believe in collective punishment now?"

A cultivator chimed in, "You claim their hands are clean just because you say so? That's nothing more than your word. Where’s your proof?"

"You claim they’re murderers—isn't that just your word?" Wei Wuxian fired back. "Shouldn't you be the one presenting evidence first? Why turn around and demand it from me?"

The man shook his head vigorously, wearing an exaggerated look of this rogue is completely unreasonable.

Another cultivator let out a cold laugh. "When the Wen Clan butchered our families, they were a thousand times more sadistic! They didn't show us an ounce of honor—why the hell should we show them any?!"

Wei Wuxian smiled faintly. "I see. Because the Wen Clan did evil, anyone bearing the surname Wen is fair game for execution? That doesn't add up. Plenty of clans that defected from Qishan are thriving right now. Aren't several clan leaders sitting right in this room former vassals of the Wen Clan?"

The sect leaders called out paled instantly, shifting uncomfortably in their seats.

Wei Wuxian’s smile vanished. "If simply carrying the surname Wen makes a person fair game for anyone's petty target practice—guilt and innocence be damned—does that mean I can butcher every single one of them right here and now?"

Before the words cleared his throat, his hand snapped down, resting directly over Chenqing.

In an instant, the sheer weight of memory crashed down upon the hall. The suffocating terror of endless skies choked by black smoke, the mountain of rotting dead, the stench of copper and ash—every horror of the war flooded their skulls at once. Cultivators scrambled to their feet, tables scraping against stone.

Lan Wangji’s voice cut through the panic, low and heavy: "Wei Ying!"

Standing closest to him, Jin Guangyao didn't flinch. His expression remained entirely composed as he urged in a gentle whisper, "Young Master Wei, please, let us not be rash. Everything can be reasoned through."

Jin Guangshan was on his feet now, terror, rage, and humiliation warring across his face. "Wei Wuxian! S-Sect Leader Jiang isn't here, and you dare run wild like this?!"

Wei Wuxian snarled, "You think having him here would stop me?! If I set my mind to killing someone, who could stand in my way? Who would even dare?!"

Lan Wangji’s words fell like heavy stone: "Wei Ying. Lower Chenqing."

Wei Wuxian glanced sideways. In those pale, glass-like eyes, he caught a reflection of his own face—twisted, dark, and bordering on feral. He jerked his head away, barking, "Jin Zixun!"

Jin Guangshan panicked. "Zixun!"

Wei Wuxian’s voice dropped to a lethal purr. "Cut the crap. You all know my patience has a short fuse. Where are they? You’ve wasted enough of my breath—I'm giving you three counts. Three!"

Jin Zixun tried to grit his teeth and hold the line, but catching Jin Guangshan’s pale, sweat-slicked face, a cold dread seized his gut.

"Two!"

Jin Zixuan finally roared from across the hall: "...Enough! Enough of this! They're just a handful of Wen dogs—if you want to use them, take them! I have no desire to waste another second arguing over this today! Go to Qiongqi Path and dig them up yourself!"

Wei Wuxian let out a dry, chilling chuckle. "See? Was that so hard?"

He arrived like a storm, and left like a gust of wind.

The moment his silhouette vanished past the threshold, the suffocating pall hanging over the hall finally lifted. Cultivators collapsed back into their chairs in scattered clumps, cold sweat drenching their inner robes. Jin Guangshan stood frozen at the head of the room for several agonizing seconds before his temper detonated, kicking the heavy table clean over. Gilded cups and silver platters went clattering down the steps in a noisy, undignified mess.

Seeing him lose face, Jin Guangyao hurried forward to smooth things over. "Fa—"

Before the word could leave his mouth, Jin Guangshan flicked his wide sleeves and stormed out. Jin Zixun, burning with humiliation over having backed down in front of the entire cultivation world, turned to storm off in the opposite direction.

Jin Guangyao rushed over. "Zixun—"

Blinded by fury, Jin Zixun didn't even think. He reared back and hurled the cup of wine he was still clutching straight at Jin Guangyao’s chest. The dark vintage splashed across the snow-white peony crest, staining the pristine silk in an ugly, sprawling blossom.

Amidst the chaotic scramble, hardly anyone noticed the vile, unprovoked insult. Only Lan Xichen called out, appalled, "Third Brother!"

Jin Guangyao recovered instantly, waving his hands with an easy, practiced smile. "I'm fine, really, Er-ge, please remain seated."

Lan Xichen held back his critique of Jin Zixun, instead pulling a clean, white handkerchief from his sleeve and offering it forward. "You should step down and change."

Taking the silk, Jin Guangyao dabbed at the dark stain, offering a bitter, helpless chuckle. "I can't walk away right now."

He was the only one left to clean up this disaster; how could he possibly step away? While moving through the room soothing ruffled feathers, he sighed under his breath, looking thoroughly worn thin: "Ah, Young Master Wei is simply too impulsive. How could he speak like that in front of all these prominent families?"

Lan Wangji’s voice dropped flat and icy: "Was he wrong?"

Jin Guangyao froze for an imperceptible fraction of a second, then forced a laugh. "Haha. No. He was right. But it's precisely because he was right that he shouldn't have spoken it aloud."

Lan Xichen fell quiet, his brow furrowing with quiet gravity. "That Young Master Wei... his temperament truly has unraveled."

Hearing those words, a flicker of raw, aching pain passed through the pale depth of Lan Wangji’s eyes.

Slipping away from Koi Tower, Wei Wuxian wound through the alleys of Lanling before ducking into a secluded back lane.

"Found them," he called out. "Let's go."

Wen Qing, who had been pacing like a caged animal, bolted out from the shadows. Running on pure adrenaline and bone-deep exhaustion, her vision swam and her foot caught on a paver. Wei Wuxian caught her arm with one hand, steadying her. "Do you want me to find a place for you to rest? I can handle this alone. I swear I'll bring Wen Ning back."

Wen Qing grabbed his sleeve, desperate. "No! No! I have to go—I have to be there!"

The moment Wen Ning vanished, she had run on foot without pausing for breath all the way from Qishan to Yunmeng, going days without shutting her eyes. When she finally cornered Wei Wuxian, she had begged and pleaded like a woman possessed. Now, her lips were chapped and bloodless, her hollow eyes glassy, looking practically hollowed out.

Seeing her on the absolute brink of collapse, and knowing they had no time to sit down for a meal, Wei Wuxian bought a handful of plain steamed buns from a roadside stall and shoved them into her hands. Wen Qing knew her body was failing her; if she didn't eat, she’d drop dead on the road. Her hair hung in tangled wisps, eyes rimmed with red, tearing into the cold bread with feral, desperate chews.

Watching her, Wei Wuxian was forcefully reminded of those desperate, hunted days on the run with Jiang Cheng. He softened his tone, promising again, "It'll be fine. I'm going to get him out."

Wen Qing choked down a bite, her voice breaking into a ragged sob. "I knew I shouldn't have left him... But I had no choice! They forcibly reassigned me to another territory, and by the time I managed to slip back, Wen Ning and our entire family were gone! I knew I couldn't leave him alone!"

Wei Wuxian said, "He can handle himself."

"He can't!" she sobbed, completely unraveling. "A-Ning has been timid and soft-spoken since he was small! He's terrified of conflict! He wouldn't even recruit retainers with strong personalities, surrounding himself with gentle, subservient people just like him! If something happens and I'm not there, he has no idea what to do!"

Back when Wei Wuxian had parted ways with her, carrying a wounded Jiang Cheng on his back, Wen Qing had stood tall with proud defiance, telling him: No matter how this war ends, from this moment on, we owe each other nothing. We are square. That untouchable pride had been burned into his memory. Yet last night, she had gripped his hands so tightly her knuckles went white, on the verge of falling to her knees, weeping: Wei Wuxian... Wei Wuxian, Young Master Wei, please help me! I have no one else to turn to... you have to help me save A-Ning! I have nowhere else to go!

That proud maiden was gone, reduced to ash.

Qiongqi Path was an ancient trail snaking through a narrow mountain gorge. Legend held that it was the very ground where Wen Mao, the founder of the Qishan Wen Sect, made his name. Hundreds of years ago, he had engaged in a brutal battle against an ancient beast for eighty-one grueling days, finally felling the creature in this pass. That primordial beast was the Qiongqi—an entity of chaotic malice that punished the righteous and rewarded the wicked, devouring loyal, honest men while blessing the corrupt. Whether the myth held any water, or was merely inflated propaganda spun by later Wen patriarchs to deify their forefather, was lost to time.

Over the centuries, the rugged canyon had transitioned from a treacherous pass into a scenic monument dedicated to ancient glory. Following the war, the sects carved up Qishan's carcass, and Qiongqi Path was swallowed into the Lanling Jin treasury. The towering canyon walls had originally been etched with massive murals recounting Wen Mao's legendary exploits; having seized the land, the Jin Clan naturally couldn't allow monuments to Wen glory to stand. A massive renovation was underway—which simply meant chiseling the rock faces clean, scrubbing away every trace of the murals, and carving their own clan crests over the stone. And, naturally, christening the gorge with a brand-new name to glorify the heroism of Lanling Jin.

An engineering feat of this scale demanded endless hard labor. And for heavy labor, no candidates were more expendable than the Wen prisoners of war.

By the time the two reached Qiongqi Path, night had settled, a cold, needle-like drizzle drifting from the dark sky. Wen Qing stumbled through the muck at Wei Wuxian’s heel, shivering violently as if chilled to her marrow; Wei Wuxian had to reach out to steady her every few paces. At the mouth of the valley stood a row of hastily erected wooden shacks where the laborers were penned at night.

Through the curtain of rain, Wei Wuxian spotted a hunched, frail silhouette slowly dragging its boots along the path, hauling a massive war banner. Drawing closer, the banner-bearer turned out to be a frail, trembling old woman. Strapped to her back with strips of worn linen was a wide-eyed toddler, solemnly gnawing on his own fingers. The grandmother struggled beneath the weight of the massive staff, pausing every few steps to catch her breath, lowering the banner into the mud.

Seeing her, Wen Qing’s eyes burned scarlet. "Granny! It's me!"

The old woman’s eyes and ears were failing her; she couldn't make out the face or the voice through the dark, only registering that someone was approaching. Terrified of a beating, she frantically hoisted the heavy staff back onto her shoulder, trembling with dread.

Wen Qing lunged forward, snatching the pole from her grip. "What is this?! What are they making you do?!"

Emblazoned across the heavy cloth was the great sunburst crest of Qishan Wen—now defaced by a massive, dripping cross of red paint, the edges frayed and ripped to shreds. Since the war ended, countless people had been branded "Wen remnants," subjected to endless, cruel humiliations under the guise of "moral reflection." Wei Wuxian knew instantly: the old woman was far too frail for stone-hauling, so the overseers had devised this twisted chore instead, forcing her to march back and forth bearing the defaced banner to degrade herself.

The old woman flinched in terror. Squinting through the gloom, she finally recognized the face before her, her mouth dropping open.

Wen Qing pleaded, "Granny, where is A-Ning?! Where is Fourth Uncle?! Where is A-Ning?!"

The grandmother cast a fearful glance at Wei Wuxian, not daring to utter a sound, merely pointing a trembling finger toward the dark mouth of the canyon. Leaving the banner behind, Wen Qing bolted into the pass.

Flaring torches lined both sides of the gorge, sputtering against the damp mist as they illuminated hundreds of silhouettes trudging along the rocky trail under crushing slabs of stone.

The prisoners were hollow-eyed and ashen, their steps dragging through the mud. They were forbidden from channeling spiritual energy or using tools—partly out of the Jin Clan's paranoia, and partly for the cruelty of punishment. A dozen overseers shielded themselves beneath black umbrellas, barking curses as they patrolled on horseback.

Wen Qing threw herself into the rain, her eyes frantically sweeping over every dirt-caked, exhausted face. An overseer spotted her, raising his whip with a sharp bark: "Where did you crawl out of?! Who gave you permission to wander in here?!"

Wen Qing cried out, "I'm looking for someone! Please, I'm looking for my brother!"

Spurring his mount closer, the guard drew an iron rod from his saddle, brandishing it in her face. "I don't give a damn who you're looking for! Get lost! Move, or—"

He froze. Standing right behind the young woman was a youth draped in pitch-black robes. The words knotted in his throat.

The young man was strikingly handsome, but the look in his eyes was pure, arctic poison. A visceral shudder raced down the overseer's spine. A heartbeat later, he realized the youth wasn't glaring at him—he was staring at the iron brand in his hand.

The tool was identical to the branding irons used by the Wen enforcers back in the day, save for one detail: the sunburst emblem at the tip had been swapped for the peony crest of Lanling Jin.

Wei Wuxian’s eyes narrowed, a lethal glint flashing through his pupils. Several overseers recognized that face; color draining from their cheeks, they quietly reined their mounts back, whispering frantically among themselves. No one dared block Wen Qing's path now.

She ran through the mud, screaming into the rain: "A-Ning! A-Ning!"

Her desperate cries echoed off the sheer cliffs, met only by the patter of cold rain. If Wen Ning had been anywhere in this valley, he would have sprinted out to meet her the second he heard her voice. The overseers dismounted quietly, clustering together as they eyed Wei Wuxian, paralyzed over whether to greet him or run.

Wen Qing lunged toward them. "Where are the Wen cultivators brought in over the last few days?!"

The guards exchanged evasive glances. After an awkward pause, an overseer with a round, deceptively honest face spoke up in an agreeable tone: "Every laborer here is a Wen cultivator, miss. New groups are brought in daily."

Wen Qing’s voice cracked. "My brother! Jin Zixun brought him here! He... he’s about this tall, quiet, stammers when he speaks..."

The man sighed, waving a hand. "Look, miss, there are hundreds of people here. How are we supposed to keep track of who stammers and who doesn't?"

Wen Qing stamped her foot in pure agony. "I know he's here!"

The round-faced guard offered a placating smile. "Don't panic, miss. Other clans stop by all the time to requisition cultivators for their own projects. Maybe someone transferred him out a few days ago? Sometimes people slip away during the night roll call too..."

"He wouldn't run!" she cried. "Granny and the rest are still here—he would never leave them behind!"

"Why don't you look around yourself?" the guard suggested casually. "Everyone here is accounted for. If you can't find him in the canyon, our hands are tied."

Wei Wuxian spoke, his voice cutting through the mist: "Everyone is accounted for?"

The overseers stiffened. The round-faced guard turned, clearing his throat. "Yes, sir."

"Fine," Wei Wuxian said flatly. "I'll accept that everyone who's breathing is accounted for. What about the rest?"

Wen Qing swayed on her feet.

The opposite of "breathing" was, without question, "dead."

The guard broke into a nervous sweat. "You can't say things like that, Young Master! They might be Wen cultivators, but nobody here has the guts to take a life—"

Wei Wuxian didn't even blink. His fingers closed around the dark flute at his waist.

The prisoners hauling stone nearby let out terrified yelps, dropping their boulders and scrambling backward into the mud. Within seconds, a massive perimeter cleared around him.

The captives didn't recognize his face. During the Sunshot Campaign, any Wen cultivator unfortunate enough to cross paths with Wei Wuxian met a single, absolute end: total annihilation. The only Wen cultivators who knew his face were the fierce corpses currently marching under his command. But that black flute, with its blood-red tassel, and the black-clad youth wielding it had long become the ultimate nightmare of their clan.

Whispers tore through the gorge: "The Ghost Flute... Chenqing!"

Wei Wuxian brought the bamboo to his lips. A sharp, piercing note tore through the night sky like a whistling arrow, cleaving through the driving rain. The sound rippled down the valley, vibrating against the stone.

With a single note, Wei Wuxian lowered the flute. Hands hanging loose at his sides, a cold smirk played across his lips, letting the rain soak through his dark hair and robes.

A moment later, a voice called out in the dark: "What... what is that sound?"

Shrieks erupted from the fringes of the crowd as laborers tumbled backward, tearing a wide opening in the ranks.

Through the pouring rain, a dozen ragged silhouettes emerged, swaying unsteadily on their feet. Tall, short, men, women—some exhaling the foul stench of early rot.

Standing at the front, eyes still wide open, was Wen Ning.

His skin was waxy and bloodless, his pupils blown wide and vacant. The dark blood crusted at the corner of his lips had congealed into an ugly, rust-colored stain. His chest lay completely still, his ribcage visibly collapsed on one side.

A single glance was enough to tell anyone with eyes that this boy was dead. Yet Wen Qing refused to believe it, lunging forward with trembling hands to seize his wrist, hunting for a pulse.

She clutched his cold skin for several agonizing seconds, then collapsed, weeping violently.

She had spent days running until her feet bled, driven mad by terror, only to arrive too late to see her brother draw his final breath.

Wen Qing sobbed hysterically, her fingers frantically tracing the shattered ribs beneath his robes, desperately trying to knit the crushed bone together—chasing an impossible sliver of life. Her delicate face twisted into something agonizing and raw. When grief tears a soul down to the bone, there is no beauty left in the crying.

Before her brother's stiff corpse, the last scrap of her pride shattered into dust.

Overwhelmed, her vision went black and she crumpled to the mud. Wei Wuxian stepped up, catching her before she hit the ground, cradling her head against his chest. He closed his eyes.

When he opened them again, his voice was chillingly level: "Who killed him?"

There was no heat in his tone, no outward roar of fury—only a quiet, suffocating gravity.

Thinking they had an out, the round-faced overseer clung to his story, stammering, "Young Master Wei, you can't throw accusations around like that! No one here dared lay a hand on him! He was careless while hauling stone, lost his footing, and took a tumble down the cliff!"

Wei Wuxian murmured, "No one dared lay a hand on him? Truly?"

The overseers chimed in together, nodding frantically: "Absolute truth!"

"We swear it!"

Wei Wuxian offered a thin smile. "Ah. I understand."

He paused, adding with deliberate, measured cruelty: "Because they are Wen dogs. And Wen dogs aren't people. So putting them down doesn't count as murder. Isn't that what you're saying?"

The guard’s jaw slacked, the exact thought he’d been nursing silently laid bare for all to hear.

Wei Wuxian continued, "Or do you honestly believe I can't tell how a corpse met its end?"

The overseers froze, the creeping realization dawning on them that they were cornered. Wei Wuxian kept that faint smile pinned in place. "You'd better step forward and confess right now. Tell me who did it. Otherwise... I'll have to adopt a policy of slaughtering the innocent rather than letting the guilty slip away. If I butcher every last one of you, I'm guaranteed not to miss."

Their scalps went numb with cold dread. The lead overseer stammered, "The Yunmeng Jiang Clan and the Lanling Jin Clan are allies right now! You can't possibly—"

Wei Wuxian looked at him, genuine amusement dancing in his eyes. "You've got some nerve. Are you threatening me?"

The man waved his hands frantically. "No, no, I wouldn't dare!"

"Congratulations," Wei Wuxian said softly. "You've officially burned through the last shred of my patience. Since you refuse to speak... I'll let him answer for himself."

As if waiting for that very command, Wen Ning’s stiff corpse jerked upright, snapping his chin up.

Before the two closest overseers could even shriek, two iron-plated hands clamped clean around their throats.

Wen Ning hoisted the squat guards high into the air without an ounce of effort, the ring of onlookers scrambling backward in a wide circle. The round-faced guard shrieked, "Young Master Wei! Young Master Wei, mercy! If you act rashly, the consequences will be irreversible!"

The rain grew torrential, streams of water washing relentlessly down Wei Wuxian’s pale cheeks.

Spinning on his heel, he slammed a hand onto Wen Ning’s shoulder, roaring into the storm: "Wen Qionglin!"

In response, a deafening, inhuman roar tore from Wen Ning’s throat, vibrating through the canyon until everyone's eardrums throbbed with agony.

Wei Wuxian ground out every syllable: "Whoever made you like this—give them the exact same end. I grant you that right. Settle the ledger!"

The moment the words landed, Wen Ning brought the two guards together with savage force.

Crack!

Their skulls collided like two overripe melons, detonating into a grotesque shower of crimson and grey matter.

The butchery broke what little order remained. Screams of sheer terror echoed down the gorge, horses rearing and whinnying as laborers fled in blind panic. Wei Wuxian scooped Wen Qing up into his arms, cutting through the stampeding mob as if strolling through a private garden. He seized the reins of a riderless horse and was about to mount when a frail laborer called out from behind a wagon.

"...Master Wei!"

Wei Wuxian glanced back. "What?"

The man’s voice shook, pointing a trembling hand toward the dark cliffs. "A-At the far end of the valley... there's a shack. They use it to... lock people up and beat them. The ones who don't survive are dragged out back and buried. The ones you're looking for... there might still be some alive inside..."

Wei Wuxian nodded curtly. "Thank you."

Following the direction, he located a ramshackle wooden shed tucked against the rock face. Shifting Wen Qing into one arm, he kicked the door clean off its hinges.

Inside sat a dozen battered cultivators huddled in the corner, covered in cuts, bruised purple and bleeding from split lips. The violent breach sent them scrambling in terror. Catching sight of Wen Qing slumped in his arms, several disciples forgot their broken ribs, throwing themselves forward with desperate cries: "Lady Qing!"

One yelled defensively, "Who... who are you?! What did you do to the Branch Leader?!"

"Nothing," Wei Wuxian replied flatly. "Which of you were under Wen Ning? Cut the chatter and get outside!"

The disciples exchanged bewildered looks, but seeing Wei Wuxian turn to leave, they had no choice but to haul each other up and stumble out behind him. The moment they cleared the threshold, the slaughter unfolding across the gorge hit them like a hammer.

Wei Wuxian called out, "Find horses, quickly!"

A middle-aged man stammered, "Wait, our Young Master Wen Ning..."

A severed head came hurtling through the air, tumbling past his boots. The group whipped their heads around, freezing at the sight: Wen Ning had pinned a twitching, headless corpse to the dirt, digging his bare hands into the man's exposed viscera.

Wei Wuxian barked, "Enough!"

A low, ravenous snarl rumbled in Wen Ning’s throat, seemingly unsatisfied. Wei Wuxian pressed his fingers to his lips, whistling a sharp, piercing command: "Rise!"

Wen Ning straightened up instantly.

Wei Wuxian turned back to the survivors. "What are you standing around for?! Mount up! You expect me to summon flying swords for you?!"

One of the cultivators remembered the elderly, scrambling to bring the grandmother and the toddler over, hoisting them onto a horse. Carrying the unconscious Wen Qing, Wei Wuxian swung into the saddle. In the chaos, they had only managed to round up a dozen mounts; with two or three people crowded onto each beast, space was tight. The old woman couldn't manage the reins alone while clinging to the child.

Seeing her struggle, Wei Wuxian reached an arm out. "Hand him here."

The grandmother shook her head frantically, while the toddler clamped his tiny arms around her neck, terrified. Reaching down, Wei Wuxian plucked the boy up by his collar, tucking him securely under his arm.

The old woman gasped in horror: "A-Yuan! A-Yuan!"

Little A-Yuan was young, but old enough to sense the danger; he didn't cry, merely gnawing furiously on his fingers, sneaking wide-eyed, terrified glances up at the man holding him.

Wei Wuxian dug his heels into the stallion's flanks, shouting into the wind: "Move!"

Taking the lead, he spurred his mount into a gallop. A dozen horses thundered behind him, disappearing into the dark, rain-swept night.
